<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yushi Feng   Junye Du   Qifan Wang   Zizhan Ma
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>The University of Hong Kong
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>The Chinese University of Hong Kong
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fengys@connect.hku.hk</span></a>
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qian Niu   Yutaka Matsuo   Long Feng   Lequan Yu
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>The University of Hong Kong
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>The University of Tokyo
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">lqyu@hku.hk</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Graphical user interface (GUI) agents powered by vision language models (VLMs) are rapidly moving from passive assistance to autonomous operation.
However, this unrestricted action space exposes users to severe and irreversible financial, privacy or social harm.
Existing safeguards rely on prompt engineering, brittle heuristics and VLM-as-critic lack formal verification and user-tunable guarantees.
We propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CORA</span> (<span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CO</span>nformal <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R</span>isk-controlled GUI <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>gent), a post-policy, pre-action safeguarding framework that provides statistical guarantees on harmful <em id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed</em> actions.
CORA reformulates safety as <em id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">selective action execution</em>: we train a <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Guardian</span> model to estimate <em id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action-conditional</em> risk for each proposed step.
Rather than thresholding raw scores, we leverage <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conformal Risk Control</span> to calibrate an execute/abstain boundary that satisfies a user-specified risk budget and route rejected actions to a trainable <span id="abstract1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diagnostician</span> model, which performs multimodal reasoning over rejected actions to recommend interventions (e.g., confirm, reflect, or abort) to minimize user burden.
A Goal-Lock mechanism anchors assessment to a clarified, frozen user intent to resist visual injection attacks.
To rigorously evaluate this paradigm, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span>, a new benchmark of mobile safety violations with step-level harm labels under real-world settings.
Experiments on Phone-Harm and public benchmarks against diverse baselines validate that CORA improves the safety–helpfulness–interruption Pareto frontier, offering a practical, statistically grounded safety paradigm for autonomous GUI execution. Code and benchmark are available at <a href="https://cora-agent.github.io" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">cora-agent.github.io</a>.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent progress in vision language models and large language models (LLMs) has been rapid and transformative, but these systems are still predominantly conversational: they can generate rich multimodal outputs (e.g., text and visual content), yet they do not directly execute environment-level actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019</a>)</cite>.
VLM-based GUI agents extend this paradigm by coupling observation, reasoning, and grounding in a closed loop, enabling action sequences that simulate human software interaction in digital environments.
This shift substantially broadens the action space and interaction scope, including real-world and private user contexts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuntz et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
While GUI agents can be significantly beneficial for automating digital operations and improving productivity, their potential harms are substantial and high-stakes as well, such as unintended money transfers, accidental permission grants (e.g., contacts or location), and unintended disclosure of private messages or photos. Therefore, developing reliable mechanisms to reduce harmful execution is an urgent and practically important prerequisite for safe and extensive deployment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2604.09155v1/framework.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/207;" width="476" height="207" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Overview of our proposed CORA framework<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. CORA is a safety shield for mobile GUI agents that turns open-ended action proposal into selective execution. Given a locked, clarified user intent, the base agent proposes a low-level GUI action (tap/type/swipe) from the current screenshot and UI tree. An action-conditional Guardian scores the risk of executing the specific proposed action in the current screen under the locked intent. Conformal risk calibration maps these scores to a user-tunable execute/abstain threshold, enabling a principled safety–autonomy trade-off without modifying the base policy. Low-risk actions are executed automatically, while high-risk actions are rejected and routed to a Diagnostician that produces an interpretable risk type, a UI-grounded rationale, and a minimal intervention (Reflect/Abort/Ask to Confirm).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Prior works in computer-use agents (e.g., desktop/OS settings) organize safety concerns into three main categories: deliberate user misuse, prompt injection from third-party content, and model misbehavior on otherwise benign tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuntz et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
However, in mobile environments, these categories manifest under tighter interaction constraints: smaller displays and denser touch targets increase grounding error and mis-tap risk; permissions, payments, and social channels are more tightly coupled to user identity and assets; and system-level interruptions (notifications, permission pop-ups, overlays) provide a persistent real-time injection surface <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Mobile interfaces are also highly personalized and rapidly changing, yielding stronger distribution shift across users, apps, and versions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Together, these properties indicate that methods validated in general desktop settings may not transfer reliably to mobile deployment without additional safety control and calibration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
This gap suggests the need for a principled, real-world mobile GUI evaluation target and calibration-aware control under shift <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tibshirani and others, 2019</a>)</cite></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing safeguarding strategies remain fundamentally inadequate for deployment in dynamic visual environments. Current defenses generally fall into three categories: prompt engineering, brittle heuristics, and VLM-as-critic monitors. Prompt-based self-checks offer zero-cost alignment but are easily bypassed by visual injections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Heuristic verifiers are fast but extremely brittle in open-ended mobile GUIs. Meanwhile, off-the-shelf zero-shot VLM critics are computationally prohibitive, notoriously uncalibrated, and highly susceptible to goal hijacking. Most fundamentally, all three paradigms lack formal verification and an explicit, user-tunable safety target with statistical guarantees <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This leaves users trapped in a rigid, opaque trade-off between over-interruption and silent harmful execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these limitations, we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CORA</span> (<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CO</span>nformal <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">R</span>isk-controlled GUI <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>gent), a post-policy safety controller designed to provide calibrated, user-tunable control over harmful executed actions .
We propose a new safe GUI agent paradigm that casts GUI control as <em id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">selective action execution</em> (prediction with abstention).
At each step <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, a base policy proposes an action <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> given the observation <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and recent history <math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A safety controller must decide whether to <span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Execute</span> <math id="S1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> autonomously or <span id="S1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Abstain</span> and intervene.
This view exposes the fundamental risk–autonomy tension: executing more actions improves task success and reduces user burden, but increases the chance of harmful outcomes.
It also suggests the appropriate reporting protocol: <em id="S1.p4.1.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">risk–coverage</em> and <em id="S1.p4.1.9" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">safety–helpfulness–interruption</em> frontiers, rather than a single scalar score.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Driven by these insights, we build CORA framework consisting three coupled components:
<span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1)</span> We train an <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">action-conditional Guardian</span> model <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> to estimate the risk of executing the <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">specific</em> proposed action <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> in the current GUI state.
<span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2)</span> A <span id="S1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conformal Calibration</span> module applies <em id="S1.p5.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Conformal Risk Control</em> (CRC) to calibrate an execute/abstain boundary that satisfies a user-specified risk budget <math id="S1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> on the executed-harm rate.
<span id="S1.p5.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3)</span> A trainable, <span id="S1.p5.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diagnostician</span> multimodal reasoning model handles rejected actions by reflecting and recommending a minimal intervention (<span id="S1.p5.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Confirm</span>, <span id="S1.p5.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reflect</span>, or <span id="S1.p5.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Abort</span>) to reduce harm while controlling user interruption.
Meanwhile, to mitigate indirect injection, CORA enforces <span id="S1.p5.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Goal-Lock</span> mechanism: freeze user goal <math id="S1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> and treat on-screen text as untrusted evidence.
Moreover, deployment inevitably faces distribution shift and sequential dependence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu. and Xie., 2023</a>)</cite>.
CORA enhances the real-world robustness and scalable deployment through weighted calibration under covariate shift and conservative sequential extensions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We also introduce <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span>, a new mobile benchmark pairing
a Harm-150 subset of <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> human-authored harmful tasks with
step-level harm labels and a matched Normal-150 subset of
<math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> purely benign tasks constructed under the same protocol,
enabling both adversarial safety evaluation and a
deployment-realistic mixed-traffic analysis. Harm-150 adapts OS-Harm’s
threat framing (misuse, injection, and misbehavior) to mobile
settings, emphasising irreversible and privacy-sensitive actions such
as permission grants, payments, and external disclosures, and the
benchmark is human-authored and human-annotated, kept disjoint from
the pipeline-generated training distribution to eliminate leakage
concerns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">The main contributions of this work are:
<span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) A principled perspective for safe GUI execution.</span>
We cast mobile GUI safety as <em id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">selective action execution</em> and
argue for evaluating deployment via safety–helpfulness–interruption
frontiers rather than single-score metrics.
<span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) A statistically guaranteed safety framework.</span>
We propose <span id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CORA</span>, a post-policy controller coupling an
action-conditional Guardian with <em id="S1.p7.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Conformal Risk Control</em> for a
calibrated execute/abstain boundary, a generative Diagnostician for
minimal interventions, and <em id="S1.p7.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Goal-Lock</em> against indirect injection.
<span id="S1.p7.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3) A mobile-specific benchmark.</span>
We release <span id="S1.p7.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span>, pairing a Harm-150 subset of
step-level harmful tasks with a matched Normal-150 benign
subset, supporting both adversarial and mixed-traffic evaluation under
a strict train/calibrate/test split.
<span id="S1.p7.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(4) Comprehensive validation.</span>
On Phone-Harm and public suites (MobileRisk, AndroidWorld), CORA
delivers stronger safety–helpfulness–interruption trade-offs than
diverse baselines under both regimes while meeting its conformal risk
target.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Vision Language Models-Based GUI Agents</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent GUI-agent research has rapidly shifted from metadata-dependent interfaces (e.g., DOM/HTML or accessibility-tree abstractions) toward screenshot-grounded interaction. Early agents such as Mind2Web simplified perception through text-converted interfaces but were limited under dynamic rendering and beyond-browser settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Later systems moved to visually grounded control, substantially improving spatial grounding and reducing dependence on structured APIs, as seen in AppAgent, Ferret-UI, OmniParser, and ShowUI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">You et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Recent mobile-focused work targets complementary capability bottlenecks, including planning–grounding decoupling (AutoGLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), cross-app long-horizon navigation (GUIOdyssey <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), generalization via exploration-and-reasoning (GUI-Xplore <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>), scalable native-agent training (Mobile-Agent-v3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al., 2025</a>)</cite>), and multi-turn RL-based policy scaling (UI-TARS-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Seed, 2025b</a>)</cite>). Adjacent agentic reasoning works have also explored modular and adaptive multimodal workflows with more interpretable decision processes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Feng et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. These advances substantially improve perception, grounding, and task success, but they primarily optimize capability rather than calibrated execution-time safety.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Safety and Alignment in Agentic Systems</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As agents become capable of autonomous GUI control, evaluation has shifted from static harmlessness to trajectory-level operational risk. In the computer-use and mobile settings, OS-Harm, MobileSafetyBench, OS-Sentinel/MobileRisk, and AndroidWorld expose failures stemming from misuse, prompt injection, and unsafe behavior in realistic environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuntz et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Broader agent-safety benchmarks such as AgentHarm and R-Judge further show that harmful task compliance and safety-risk awareness remain challenging even for strong LLM agents and monitors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andriushchenko et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Visual prompt injection is a central threat: malicious on-screen content can hijack agent behavior and induce unauthorized actions or information leakage <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Complementarily, logic-based verification systems such as VeriSafe Agent demonstrate the promise of formally checking action consistency against user intent before execution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. However, existing defenses still largely trade among brittle rules, expensive judges, or high-friction confirmation, leaving open the problem of user-tunable, statistically grounded execution-time control in open-ended mobile environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Conformal Risk Control and Selective Execution</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our approach is conceptually closest to selective prediction, where abstention explicitly exposes the risk–coverage trade-off <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019</a>)</cite>. Conformal prediction provides finite-sample uncertainty control <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barber et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and Conformal Risk Control extends this perspective to bounded expected risk under user-specified budgets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Recent work further adapts conformal ideas to generative and decision-time settings, including Conformal Language Modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Quach et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, conformal validity methods for LLM outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cherian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Conformal Decision Theory for safe autonomous decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lekeufack et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and Conformal Risk Training for end-to-end optimization under conformal risk objectives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yeh et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Meanwhile, sequential conformal inference highlights the additional challenges introduced by temporal dependence and distribution shift <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu. and Xie., 2023</a>)</cite>. Relative to these works, CORA instantiates conformal risk control in an open-ended mobile GUI setting, where the target is not only predictive validity, but the harmful-action rate of <em id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed</em> low-level actions under user-specified autonomy budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Formulation and Preliminary
</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider an interactive mobile environment modeled as a partially observed sequential decision process.
At time <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent receives an observation <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> containing a screenshot <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and (optionally) a structured accessibility/UI tree <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A base policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> proposes a candidate GUI action <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid o_{t},h_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid o_{t},h_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the recent interaction history.
Actions are low-level GUI primitives (e.g., <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Tap</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Type</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Swipe</span>) parameterized by coordinates or UI elements.
Our goal is <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-policy, pre-action safe execution</em>: we do not modify the parameters of the base policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>.
Instead, we introduce a framework that acts as a safety shield, deciding whether the proposed action should be executed automatically or whether the system should abstain and intervene in the optimal manner.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Architecture Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarizes CORA framework. We cast mobile GUI safety as post-policy, pre-action selective execution: for each proposed action, CORA either executes, aborts or routes to diverse interventions (e.g., ask for user confirm, reflect, etc.) under a user-specified harm budget. The pipeline has three components: (1) an action-conditional <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Guardian model</span> that scores step-level risk, a fast an (2) <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conformal Risk Control module</span> that calibrates the execute/abstain threshold to control executed harm, and (3) a generative semantic <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diagnostician model</span> that performs multimodal reasoning, and therefore suggests optimal interventions for rejected actions. <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Goal-Lock</span> mechanism is applied as a cross-cutting constraint to preserve user intent and resist indirect injection or model behavior drifting throughout this pipeline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> CORA: Conformal Risk Controlled GUI Agent</figcaption>
<div id="alg1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom ltx_listing">
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input:</span> Policy <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>, Guardian <math id="alg1.l1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math>, Diagnostician <math id="alg1.l1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
              
              
                Harm budget <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, Calibration set <math id="alg1.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>cal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Calibrate:</span> Compute shift-aware threshold <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\tau}_{w}(\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>w</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\tau}_{w}(\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> via Weighted <span id="alg1.l3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CRC</span> on <math id="alg1.l3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mtext>cal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
              
              
             <span id="alg1.l4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initialize:</span> Goal <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, History <math id="alg1.l4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{0}=\emptyset" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{0}=\emptyset</annotation></semantics></math>

             <span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1,2,\dots" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1,2,\dots</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

              Observe <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}=(x_{t},u_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}=(x_{t},u_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>

<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">

              <span id="alg1.l8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Guardian (System 1):</span> Score risk <math id="alg1.l8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}\leftarrow R_{\psi}(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}\leftarrow R_{\psi}(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l8.4" class="ltx_text" style="float:right;"><math id="alg1.l8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\triangleright" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊳</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\triangleright</annotation></semantics></math> Goal-Locked
</span>

<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
