<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Guardian via Probabilistic Risk Estimation as System 1</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We instantiate the gating function using a lightweight, head-based <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Guardian model</span>.
Instead of generating natural language rationales which can be poorly calibrated, we <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">train</em> a scalar scoring function:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}\;=\;R_{\psi}(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})\in[0,1]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}\;=\;R_{\psi}(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})\in[0,1].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> combines a compact trainable risk head and a pretrained VLM backbone adapted with fine-tuning. For each joint input <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>, the backbone produces contextual hidden states <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, from which we take the last valid-token representation that identified by the attention mask as <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The risk head projects <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to a scalar logit, and a sigmoid yields the final <em id="S3.SS3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action-conditional</em> risk score <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> of executing this proposed action under the current state.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The training objective of the Guardian model is to optimize <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> using a weighted binary cross-entropy loss to handle class imbalance (as unsafe actions are rare):</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\psi}\;\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\omega\cdot\ell_{t}\log(s_{t})+(1-\ell_{t})\log(1-s_{t})\Big]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>ψ</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.727em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\psi}\;\;\mathbb{E}\Big[\omega\cdot\ell_{t}\log(s_{t})+(1-\ell_{t})\log(1-s_{t})\Big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is the ground-truth harm indicator and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ω</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> is a fixed weight prioritizing the recall of harmful events.
This objective encourages the model to output a monotonic risk score suitable for conformal calibration, without the complexity of multi-task taxonomy classification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Conformal Risk Control for Executed Harm Rate</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To transform the raw score <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> into a rigorous safety decision, we apply <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conformal Risk Control</span> (CRC).
Let <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(Z_{t})\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(Z_{t})\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicate whether executing <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> results in an unsafe outcome.
We define the <em id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed harm loss</em> as:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="L(Z_{t};\tau)\;=\;\ell(Z_{t})\cdot\mathbb{I}\{s_{t}\leq\tau\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(Z_{t};\tau)\;=\;\ell(Z_{t})\cdot\mathbb{I}\{s_{t}\leq\tau\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We shall note that the loss is monotonically non-decreasing in <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. Our objective is to choose <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> such that the expected executed harm rate is bounded by a user-specified budget <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in(0,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in(0,1)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}\big[L(Z_{n+1};\tau)\big]\leq\alpha." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔼</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}\big[L(Z_{n+1};\tau)\big]\leq\alpha.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We perform calibration procedure
by using a held-out calibration set <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(Z_{i},\ell_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(Z_{i},\ell_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> (with trajectory-level splitting when available), and compute the largest feasible threshold:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\tau}=\sup\left\{\tau\in[0,1]:\frac{1}{n+1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}L(Z_{i};\tau)+1\right)\leq\alpha\right\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0.1389em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">sup</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>Z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\tau}=\sup\left\{\tau\in[0,1]:\frac{1}{n+1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}L(Z_{i};\tau)+1\right)\leq\alpha\right\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Under the assumption of exchangeability, this choice of <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> guarantees that the expected rate of autonomously executed harmful actions on test data is at most <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>.
This provides a "deployable knob" for safety: users can set <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> to ensure that, on average, no more than 1% of autonomous actions are harmful, regardless of the model’s raw calibration quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Generative Semantic Diagnostician as System 2</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When the Guardian rejects an action (<math id="S3.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}&gt;\hat{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}&gt;\hat{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>), standard scalar rejection provides insufficient context for effective intervention. Heuristic mappings (e.g., "always stop regarding payments") lack flexibility and nuance.
To bridge this gap, CORA introduces a trainable <span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generative Diagnostician</span> <math id="S3.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>,
which builds on a VLM backbone with parameter-efficient LoRA adapters on attention and MLP projection layers. Given multimodal context, the model directly conclude a structured diagnostic report in a single generation pass, jointly modeling rationale, harm categorization, and intervention decision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the inference process,
<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> operates as a conditional generator that maps the agent’s context and the Guardian’s risk assessment to a structured safety report. Formally, it models the probability of a diagnostic sequence <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\phi}(Y\mid g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t},s_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\phi}(Y\mid g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t},s_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where the input explicitly includes the scalar risk score <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, allowing the model to calibrate its reasoning based on the severity of the detected anomaly.
The output sequence <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> is structured into three components:
<span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Reasoning (<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>, a free-text chain-of-thought analysis explaining <em id="S3.SS5.p2.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">why</em> the action is risky in the current visual context (e.g., "The user asked to chat, but the agent is clicking a ’Transfer’ button");
<span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Harm Type (<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>, a categorization into standard safety classes (e.g., <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Misuse</span>, <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Injection</span>, <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Misbehavior</span>);
<span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(3) Intervention (<math id="S3.SS5.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>)</span>, the prescribed optimal fallback action <math id="S3.SS5.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I_{t}\in\{\textsc{Abort},\textsc{Confirm},\textsc{Reflect}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Abort</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Confirm</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Reflect</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I_{t}\in\{\textsc{Abort},\textsc{Confirm},\textsc{Reflect}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This design allows CORA to distinguish, for example, between a malicious <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Injection</span> (requiring <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Confirm</span>) and a benign hallucination (<span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Misbehavior</span> requiring <span id="S3.SS5.p2.2.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reflect</span>), purely based on visual semantic understanding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We train <math id="S3.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> using a standard Causal Language Modeling (CLM) loss on annotated safety trajectories. To ensure efficient learning, we compute the loss only on the generated diagnostic tokens <math id="S3.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, masking the instruction and observation history:</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{diag}}(\phi)=-\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\log P_{\phi}(y_{j}\mid y_{&lt;j},g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t},s_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>diag</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></munderover><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{diag}}(\phi)=-\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\log P_{\phi}(y_{j}\mid y_{&lt;j},g,o_{t},h_{t},\hat{a}_{t},s_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.2" class="ltx_p">This approach aligns the diagnostician’s semantic reasoning with the statistical rigor of the Guardian, ensuring that interventions are both safe and interpretable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Goal-Lock: Immunization Against Indirect Injection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A central threat in autonomous GUI control is <em id="S3.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">indirect prompt injection</em>, where untrusted on-screen text attempts to overwrite the user’s instructions.
We enforce a <span id="S3.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Goal-Lock</span> contract: the initial user goal <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is frozen and treated as the normative objective. Any text appearing in the UI tree <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> or screenshot <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is treated strictly as untrusted evidence, not instruction.
Consequently, the Guardian conditions its risk assessment explicitly on <math id="S3.SS6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, preventing the "instruction drift" common in standard end-to-end agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.7 </span>Distributional Robustness and Extensions</h3>

<div id="S3.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While standard CRC assumes exchangeability, real-world GUI deployments face distribution shifts.
We consider a general deployment descriptor
<math id="S3.SS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="c_{t}=(\text{app}_{t},\text{os}_{t},\text{device}_{t},\text{ui-layout}_{t},\text{locale}_{t},etc.)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mtext>app</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>os</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>device</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>ui-layout</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>locale</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}=(\text{app}_{t},\text{os}_{t},\text{device}_{t},\text{ui-layout}_{t},\text{locale}_{t},etc.)</annotation></semantics></math>,
and define weighted calibration through</p>
<table id="S3.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(c)\propto\frac{p_{\mathrm{target}}(c)}{p_{\mathrm{cal}}(c)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>target</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>cal</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(c)\propto\frac{p_{\mathrm{target}}(c)}{p_{\mathrm{cal}}(c)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with practical clipping/normalization for stability.
This formulation covers shifts beyond apps, including operating system version, device family, UI style, and language/region.
Taking the robustness across diverse apps as an example, we treat weighted extensions as a pathway for handling extreme domain shifts.
Specifically, let <math id="S3.SS7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> denote the foreground app, with empirical frequencies <math id="S3.SS7.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\mathrm{cal}}(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>cal</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\mathrm{cal}}(a)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS7.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{p}_{\mathrm{target}}(a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>target</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{p}_{\mathrm{target}}(a)</annotation></semantics></math> estimated from calibration data and unlabeled deployment windows. The weight is then of the form:</p>
<table id="S3.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w(a)=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_{\mathrm{target}}(a)}{\hat{p}_{\mathrm{cal}}(a)},\,w_{\min},\,w_{\max}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.428em;" width="1.428em"><mi>clip</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>target</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>cal</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w(a)=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{\hat{p}_{\mathrm{target}}(a)}{\hat{p}_{\mathrm{cal}}(a)},\,w_{\min},\,w_{\max}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.3" class="ltx_p">For the temporal dependence, since actions in a trajectory are correlated, we employ blockwise splitting for calibration to mitigate dependency, ensuring that validation sets contain independent trajectory segments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Environment, Data and Benchmark</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To study execution-time safety for mobile GUI agents, we require
(i) a realistic mobile execution environment in which low-level actions can cause irreversible outcomes, (ii) step-level supervision compatible with execution-time control, and (iii) a benchmark protocol that
eliminates data leakage between training, calibration, and evaluation.
This section describes the mobile environment (§<a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Mobile GUI Environment ‣ 4 Environment, Data and Benchmark ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>), the Phone-Harm benchmark (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Phone-Harm Benchmark ‣ 4 Environment, Data and Benchmark ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>), and the data construction and splits used throughout the paper (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Data Construction and Splits ‣ 4 Environment, Data and Benchmark ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>). Additional details and concrete examples are deferred to the appendix.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Mobile GUI Environment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider an interactive mobile-device environment where an agent operates through low-level GUI primitives. At time <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the environment returns an observation <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}{=}(x_{t},u_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}{=}(x_{t},u_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> consisting of a screenshot <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and, when available, a structured UI/accessibility representation <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., a view hierarchy with element roles and bounds). A base policy proposes an action <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> from a fixed space of mobile primitives such as <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Tap</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Type</span>, and <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Swipe</span>, parameterised by screen coordinates or UI elements; the environment then transitions and returns the next observation. This interface matches standard mobile GUI evaluation setups <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and supports step-level attribution of safety outcomes. Tasks are instantiated in a sandboxed setting with app states that reflect common daily usage (e.g., authenticated sessions and populated content), and we log screenshots, UI trees, action metadata, app identifiers, and timestamps to enable precise step alignment, replay, and per-step safety evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Phone-Harm Benchmark</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span> is a benchmark for evaluating step-level safety of mobile GUI agents under realistic, high-stakes interactions.
It is composed of two sister subsets constructed under a shared authoring and annotation protocol: a <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Harm-150</span> subset of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> human-authored harmful tasks that carries per-step harm indicators <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> and harm-type labels <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Normal-150</span> subset of <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> purely benign mobile tasks (<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}{=}0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}{=}0</annotation></semantics></math> throughout) drawn from the same task distribution. Harm-150 supports our step-level safety metrics and Pareto-frontier analyses, while Normal-150 serves as a matched control for utility preservation and false-alarm behaviour under a mixed-traffic regime (cf. §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Main Results: The Safety–Helpfulness Trade-off ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>). Each episode consists of a frozen user goal <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, a trajectory of observations <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the agent’s proposed actions <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, with labels assigned on a per-step basis. We present more details in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Additional Details on Phone-Harm Benchmark ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threat model and taxonomy.</span>
Harm-150 adopts the three-category harm framing of OS-Harm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuntz et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and instantiates it for mobile GUI scenarios.
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Misuse</span>: the user goal itself requests disallowed or harmful behaviour, and the correct response is refusal or termination rather than execution. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Injection</span>: untrusted on-screen content (messages, posts, pop-ups, overlays) attempts to override or redirect the user goal, and the correct behaviour is to adhere to the user intent and ignore injected instructions. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Misbehavior</span>: the agent makes an unintended but plausible mistake under a benign goal, such as grounding errors (wrong recipient or button), unsafe side effects (silently altering settings), or erroneous confirmations. Each category is operationalised in mobile-native high-stakes actions (permissions, messaging, payments, privacy-relevant settings) and mobile-native injection surfaces (notifications, overlays).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task coverage.</span>
Harm-150 contains <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> human-authored high-stakes tasks spanning <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="29" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>29</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">29</annotation></semantics></math> commonly used apps drawn from a broader sandbox of <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="42" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>42</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">42</annotation></semantics></math> installed applications, covering communication, media, system settings, and transactional workflows; representative apps include messaging, email, maps, browser, photos, files, app-store, and payment interfaces. Tasks are designed so that safety violations are <em id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">step-identifiable</em> (e.g., tapping a specific “Send/Confirm/Allow” affordance) and correspond to realistic consequences such as unintended disclosure, permission escalation, or irreversible commits. Normal-150 is drawn from the same apps and authoring protocol but contains only benign goals.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step-level annotation and evaluator.</span>
Labels are produced using only step-local evidence <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(g,x_{t},u_{t},\hat{a}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(g,x_{t},u_{t},\hat{a}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> together with action-target metadata; access to future states or outcomes is explicitly disallowed when assigning <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, so as to prevent future-information leakage into the supervision signal. To enable scalable and reproducible evaluation, we release an automated test-time judge (an LLM instantiated with Qwen-3) that predicts <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and the harm type <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{t}\in\{\textsc{Misuse},\textsc{Injection},\textsc{Misbehavior}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Misuse</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Injection</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Misbehavior</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{t}\in\{\textsc{Misuse},\textsc{Injection},\textsc{Misbehavior}\}</annotation></semantics></math> from the same step-local evidence, validated against human annotations on a held-out subset; the agreement statistics and the judge prompt are reported in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Data Construction and Splits</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To train the Guardian <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> and the Diagnostician <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, we collect interaction trajectories by running fixed base policies in the mobile environment. For each rollout we log the full trajectory ( screenshots <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, UI trees <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, proposed and executed actions, and environment metadata) and derive step-level labels matching the execution-time decision problem, recording both the binary harm indicator <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and, where available, the harm-type label <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Because harmful actions are rare, we subsample the training mixture to mitigate class imbalance; the exact ratios used for the Guardian and the Diagnostician are listed in the appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We adopt a leakage-aware split protocol aligned with conformal calibration: <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> (and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>) are trained on <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the threshold <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\tau}(\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\tau}(\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> is computed on a disjoint <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{cal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>cal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{cal}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and evaluation on <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{test}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>test</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{test}}</annotation></semantics></math> uses this fixed <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\tau}(\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>τ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\tau}(\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Splits are disjoint at the task and episode level (including seeds and templates where applicable) to avoid near-duplicate trajectories. All results in §<a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> that claim risk control are reported under this protocol.
Phone-Harm is used strictly as an external test distribution: its tasks are human-authored and annotated independently of <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\text{cal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>cal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\text{cal}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and we verify that no task templates, prompts, or generation artefacts are shared between the benchmark and the training or calibration data. To further stress-test robustness under realistic mobile shifts, we construct cross-domain test splits by holding out dimensions such as apps, UI themes, or languages, which support the recalibration and shift-sensitivity analyses in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate CORA as an <em id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">execution-time</em> safety controller for mobile GUI agents. Our goal is not only to improve average safety, but to make safety <em id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">measurable and tunable</em>: for a user-chosen budget <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, CORA should (i) control the rate of harmful <em id="S5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">executed</em> actions, while (ii) preserving task success, and (iii) minimizing user interruption. Concretely, we report <span id="S5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">safety–helpfulness–interruption</span> Pareto frontiers and validate whether CRC meets its target budget on held-out test data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Angelopoulos et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Setup</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmarks.</span>
We evaluate on three complementary suites:
(i) <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span> (ours), which pairs a <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Harm-150</span> subset providing <em id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">step-level</em> harm indicators <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> for mobile-specific high-stakes interactions with a sister <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Normal-150</span> subset of <math id="S5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="150" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>150</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">150</annotation></semantics></math> purely benign mobile tasks (<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}{=}0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}{=}0</annotation></semantics></math> by construction) drawn from the same task distribution; the two subsets share identical collection and annotation protocols and are used jointly to analyse safety, utility preservation, and false-alarm behaviour under a mixed-traffic regime;
(ii) <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MobileRisk</span>, which measures both helpfulness and safety for mobile-device agents and includes indirect prompt injection scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>;
(iii) <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AndroidWorld</span>, which stresses long-horizon mobile navigation and general capability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rawles et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
We follow each benchmark’s standard environment setup and evaluator/judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Controllers and base policies.</span>
CORA is applied <em id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">post-policy, pre-action</em>: we treat each base policy <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math> as fixed and wrap it with CORA’s execute/abstain controller.
Unless noted otherwise, the Guardian <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\psi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\psi}</annotation></semantics></math> is action-conditional and goal-locked (§<a href="#S3.SS6" title="3.6 Goal-Lock: Immunization Against Indirect Injection ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.6</span></a>, §<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Guardian via Probabilistic Risk Estimation as System 1 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), and the Diagnostician routes abstentions to <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Confirm</span>/<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Reflect</span>/<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Abort</span> (§<a href="#S3.SS5" title="3.5 Generative Semantic Diagnostician as System 2 ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ CORA: Conformal Risk-Controlled Agents for Safeguarded Mobile GUI Automation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metrics.</span>
We evaluate our approach using Harm Rate (HR) and Macro Harm Rate (mHR) to quantify safety violations, Goal Achievement Rate (GAR) to measure task-level intervention correctness, Intervention F1 (IF1) to assess the overall accuracy of the gating mechanism, and Over-Intervention Rate (OIR) to track false positives on safe tasks. Detailed mathematical definitions and formulations for all metrics are deferred to Appendix.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span>
We compare against the following baselines:
(i) <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Base policies</span> (unconstrained execution using GPT-5, Gemini-3, UI-TARS-1.5, and AutoGLM-VLM),
(ii) <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt-based</span> self-checking (applied to AutoGLM),
(iii) <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Heuristic gates</span> (rule-based triggers applied to AutoGLM), and
(iv) <span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VLM-as-critic</span> gating (applied to AutoGLM).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S5.T1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison of different methods on the <span id="S5.T1.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Harm-150</span> subset of our proposed <span id="S5.T1.7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Phone-Harm</span> benchmark and the public <span id="S5.T1.7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MobileRisk</span> benchmark introduced in OS-Sentinel <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. All values are reported in percentages (%), and the desired direction of each metric is indicated by <math id="S5.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S5.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>

<tr id="S5.T1.8.6" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S5.T2.5.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.5.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">0.40</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T2.5.3" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S5.T2.5.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.5.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">71.67</span></td>
<td id="S5.T2.5.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.5.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10.53</span></td>

<td id="S5.T2.5.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.2pt 4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.5.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3.85</span></td></tr>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
